title: How to Make Authentic Agra-Style Kesar Petha at Home in Three Steps
excerpt: This saffron-scented ash gourd sweet, a signature delicacy of Agra, can be recreated in your own kitchen with just a handful of ingredients and a little patience.
body:
• Kesar Petha is a translucent, chewy sweet made from ash gourd (white pumpkin) soaked in saffron-infused sugar syrup — a signature delicacy of Agra.
  • The key to authentic texture lies in soaking the gourd in lime water (chuna) overnight, which firms the flesh and creates the characteristic crystalline bite.
  • The entire process takes about 24 hours of soaking plus 30-40 minutes of active cooking, and yields enough for a generous batch.

Walk through any lane near the Taj Mahal and the scent hits before the shops come into view — caramelized sugar, saffron, and the faint earthiness of ash gourd. Agra's petha has been the city's edible calling card for centuries, a translucent sweet that collapses into a soft, chewy bite. The kesar (saffron) variety, stained gold and fragrant, remains the most prized.

Making it at home requires no special equipment, just ash gourd, sugar, saffron, lime water, and time. Here is how to do it right.

Ingredients

For a batch of approximately 800 grams:

  • 500 grams ash gourd (also called white pumpkin or winter melon), peeled, deseeded, and cut into 1-inch cubes
  • 1½ cups sugar
  • ½ teaspoon food-grade lime (chuna), dissolved in 4 cups of water
  • 8-10 strands saffron (kesar), soaked in 1 tablespoon warm milk
  • 3-4 green cardamom pods, lightly crushed
  • 1 teaspoon kewra water (screwpine essence)
  • 1 teaspoon lemon juice
  • A pinch of saffron food colour (optional, for deeper hue)

Step 1: Prepare and Soak the Ash Gourd

Peel the ash gourd, remove all seeds and the soft fibrous center, and cut the firm flesh into even cubes. Prick each piece thoroughly with a fork — this allows the lime water and later the sugar syrup to penetrate to the core.

Dissolve the chuna in 4 cups of water in a large bowl. Submerge the ash gourd pieces, stir well, cover, and let them soak for a full 24 hours. Stir the mixture every 3-4 hours if possible. By morning, the pieces will have turned firm and opaque white. This step is non-negotiable — it is what gives petha its signature firm-yet-yielding texture and prevents the cubes from turning mushy during cooking.

After soaking, rinse the pieces exhaustively under running water — at least 12-15 changes of water, rubbing each piece individually. No trace of chuna should remain, or the finished sweet will taste bitter.

Step 2: Boil the Gourd

Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Add the washed ash gourd pieces and cook for 12-15 minutes, stirring occasionally. The cubes should become slightly translucent but still hold their shape — test by pressing a piece between your fingers; it should be tender but not falling apart. Drain immediately and rinse with cold water to arrest the cooking.

Step 3: Cook in Saffron Sugar Syrup

In a large, wide kadai or heavy-bottomed pan, combine the sugar with ¼ cup of water. Heat over medium flame, stirring until the sugar dissolves completely. Add the soaked saffron along with its milk, the crushed cardamom pods, and a pinch of saffron food colour if using.

Add a teaspoon of lemon juice — this prevents the syrup from crystallizing unevenly and helps remove any scum. Once the syrup reaches a rolling simmer, gently add the boiled ash gourd pieces.

Cook on medium heat for 15-20 minutes, stirring gently to avoid breaking the delicate cubes. The pieces will gradually turn translucent and golden, absorbing the saffron syrup. The syrup should reduce to a three-thread consistency — when you lift a drop between thumb and forefinger, it should form three distinct threads.

Remove from heat, add the kewra water, and gently mix. Lift the petha pieces out with a slotted spoon and spread them on a greased plate or wire rack, ensuring they don't touch each other. Let them cool completely — at least 4-6 hours — until the surface develops a light crystalline coating.

Storage and Serving

Freshly made kesar petha keeps well in an airtight container at room temperature for 4-5 days, or up to two weeks when refrigerated. Bring to room temperature before serving for the best texture. For a drier petha, let the pieces sit overnight on the rack; for a juicier version, store them with a spoonful of the remaining syrup.

The beauty of homemade petha lies in its freshness — no preservatives, no artificial sweeteners, and a depth of saffron flavour that commercial versions rarely match. For diaspora families far from Agra, it is a small way to bring the old city into the kitchen.
nri_angle: For Indians abroad craving authentic Agra petha, this straightforward home recipe brings a taste of the city's most famous sweet to diaspora kitchens worldwide.
